## The idea

Chromatic chords do not all behave like secondary dominants. *Modal mixture*
borrows a chord from the parallel major or minor key while the tonic stays
fixed. In C major, F minor is borrowed from C minor. Its A-flat usually falls
to G, giving the familiar minor-iv-to-I sound.

The blues uses another chromatic grammar. A twelve-bar blues can place dominant
sevenths on I, IV, and V. In common-practice tonal syntax, a dominant seventh
normally demands a tonic a fifth below. In blues, the seventh is part of the
sonority and voice-leading language even when the chord remains on I.

Context explains origin. Ask whether the chromatic chord points to a temporary
target, comes from the parallel mode, or belongs to a style whose chord
functions differ from the diatonic model.

## Run this

The first phrase compares major IV with borrowed minor iv. The second encodes a
twelve-bar blues in scale-degree numbers and renders it in C.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 82
use_synth :piano

[:c3, :f3, :f3, :c3].zip([:major, :major, :minor, :major]).each do |root, quality|
  play_chord chord(root, quality), release: 1.8, amp: 0.75
  sleep 2
end

sleep 2

twelve_bar = [1, 1, 1, 1, 4, 4, 1, 1, 5, 4, 1, 5]
degree_offsets = {1 => 0, 4 => 5, 5 => 7}
tonic = note(:c3)

twelve_bar.each do |degree|
  root = tonic + degree_offsets[degree]
  play_chord chord(root, :dom7), release: 1.8, amp: 0.72
  sleep 2
end
```

The A-flat in F minor darkens the return to C and falls by semitone to G. In
the blues, each chord carries a minor seventh, including C7 on the home tonic.

## Change one thing

1. Replace F minor with A-flat major before the final C. Both chords come from
   C minor and contain A-flat, but their bass motion differs. Compare the
   borrowed colour and strength of return.
2. Change every :dom7 in the blues to :major. The form remains, while the
   characteristic friction between major thirds and minor sevenths disappears.
3. Set tonic to note(:e3), then note(:a2). The numeral array and offsets stay
   fixed. Listen for the form surviving transposition while register changes
   the weight of the voicings.

## Why it works

Parallel keys share a tonic and differ in scale degrees. Borrowing from the
parallel minor introduces flattened degrees into major: flat 3, flat 6, and
flat 7 are common sources. Minor iv uses flat 6. Its semitone descent to degree
5 creates smooth voice leading into I.

Secondary dominants introduce raised pitches to target another chord. Borrowed
chords often introduce lowered pitches that colour motion toward the existing
tonic. This is a listening heuristic rather than a complete analysis, but it
helps classify the first chromatic chord in a progression.

The twelve-bar blues is stored as degrees because its form is transposable.
The renderer maps I, IV, and V to root offsets, then applies the same dominant
seventh quality. The code makes the theoretical exception visible: the I7
chord is not a mistake in the quality table. It is part of the style.

Blues performance adds rhythm, melodic blue notes, voicing, and timbre that the
block harmony omits. Keep this example spare so the harmonic pattern remains
audible. Add groove after you can identify the four-bar groups and the V-IV-I
turnaround.

The block labels are analytical claims about this particular model, not a rule
that every blues performance follows the same twelve bars or chord qualities.
When a source differs, encode what it does and record the style or recording
context instead of forcing its harmony into this array.

## Take it further

Render the same twelve-bar numeral array in C, E, and A without duplicating the
form data. Add a separate four-bar major-key phrase containing one borrowed
chord. For every chromatic pitch, comment on its source: parallel minor,
dominant seventh quality, or another named rule. The target is a progression
where you can explain why each outside note appears and hear the difference
between tonicisation and modal colour.
